Are 34,000 seats enough for a new Royals ballpark?
34
  • Kansas City Royals Analysis

Are 34,000 seats enough for a new Royals ballpark?

The new ballpark will have more limited seating than the K.

by Max Rieper
Sep 14, 2026, 2:48 PM EDT
3434Comments

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:46
Instaread

The Royals announced today they have selected a construction team with Mortenson and McCownGordon heading the project, along with local builder JE Dunn for the proposed downtown ballpark. While the project could still be subject to a public vote, the plans call for a 34,000-seat ballpark located by Crown Center.

The seating capacity would represent a 10 percent reduction from the 37,903 capacity at Kauffman Stadium, which is a 6.7 percent reduction from the 40,625 seats the stadium held until renovations in the early 2000s. At 34,000 seats, it would have a smaller capacity than any other current MLB stadium (excluding Sutter Health Park in Sacramento).

But the smaller capacity is part of a larger trend in ballparks. The new Athletics ballpark in Las Vegas is projected to have just 33,000 seats, and a new proposed Rays ballpark in St. Petersburg will have just 31,000 permanent seats. Even recent ballparks for the Braves and Rangers, both of which have capacities over 40,000, reduced the number of seats by 15 percent over their previous homes.

This comes as average attendance at MLB games is above pre-pandemic levels and on pace to rise for the fifth consecutive year. While the number of fans at games is still down from the early 2000s, they are much higher than they were in the 80s and 90s when many teams played in cavernous multi-purpose stadiums.

So what gives?

While it may seem counterintuitive, baseball teams are no longer trying to get as many people into the ballpark as possible. Instead, they are trying to get more out of the people who do show up.

For much of baseball history, stadium economics were fairly straightforward - sell as many tickets as possible, then sell those fans hot dogs, beer, peanuts, and Cracker Jack after they’re in. Even if the stadium sits half-empty for mid-week September games, teams wanted to maximize the number of fans they could accommodate for big draws.

But today, the economics of the modern ballpark are different. Teams increasingly value premium seating, clubs, suites, restaurants, bars and social spaces over another few thousand inexpensive seats in the upper deck. Those amenities take up considerably more room per customer, but they can also generate considerably more revenue. A filing in a 2014 lawsuit showed that the Royals had just 19 private suites, by far the lowest number in baseball and far below the MLB-average of 76.

Fewer seats also constrain supply, which can drive prices up. According to a study by Seatgeek and Doc’s Sports, the Royals have the sixth-cheapest tickets in baseball. The Athletics, who went from playing in a huge football stadium in Oakland to a minor league ballpark with just over 14,000 seats, suddenly had the third-most expensive ticket in baseball to watch a team with a worse record than the Royals.

Forbes estimates the Royals made $76 million in gate receipts in 2025. That is not too bad considering they finished with the fifth-worst attendance. But there is considerably more money to be made from each customer, as teams with recently-built ballparks have found. The Braves, playing at Truist Park, generated an estimated $64 in gate receipts per attendee, while the Rangers generated about $55 per attendee at Globe Life Field.

Note: Data excludes the Rays and Athletics, who played at minor league ballparks in 2025.

Does a smaller capacity make sense for the Royals?

A new ballpark must fit into a tighter location at Crown Center than the sprawling Truman Sports Complex. The anticipated ballpark district would take up 85 acres, about a fifth of the acreage at their current location. With less land available for the stadium, parking and surrounding development, designers will have an incentive to use space more efficiently rather than devote it to thousands of seats that would sit empty for much of the season.

The team has never averaged 34,000 fans per game for an entire season. Not counting home openers, the team has only had 25 total games since 2016 with 34,000 fans or more - most of those were filled with Cardinals fans. For most games, the lost seats won’t be noticed.

On the other hand, during their 2015 championship season, they drew 34,000 or more in 41 of their 81 home games. And part of the argument for moving downtown is that the Royals could draw fans who aren’t coming to Kauffman Stadium now. More than 30,000 people live downtown, while thousands more commute there for work and could more easily catch a weeknight game. If a downtown stadium succeeds in expanding the Royals’ audience, a 34,000-seat capacity that looks perfectly adequate based on recent attendance could suddenly feel a lot more limiting.

Despite potentially higher prices, a smaller stadium does not necessarily mean a worse fan experience. Fewer seats may create a more intimate environment - it is not as much fun to attend a game with thousands of empty seats. Reducing the amount of space devoted to seating can also give designers more room for wider concourses, gathering areas, restaurants and bars, standing-room viewing areas and other amenities that allow fans to move around the ballpark without losing touch with the game.

A smaller stadium would be more than enough for the Royals on most nights, and a smaller footprint could create a more intimate and enjoyable experience. But the tradeoff will become apparent when the team is good, when fewer seats will mean higher prices and some fans getting shut out. The Royals are designing a ballpark to maximize revenues to compete with other teams. A smaller stadium may make sense for the economics of modern baseball, even if Royals fans someday find themselves wishing there were more seats.

The fact of the matter is that most MLB teams do not fill 34k seats very often. The data is pretty consistent: every year, about 10 teams average 35k or more attendance. Most of those come from the same types of cities: New York, Boston, Los Angeles, Chicago, Toronto, San Francisco. You know, cities with gigantic populations and both national and international tourism.

Kansas City has never averaged 34,000 fans a game for a year. Yes, in a great year the Royals pulled in more than 34k fans a decent amount...but only half the time.

When the median home game across the league is less than 30k attendance, it makes total sense to build a stadium a little than that. But the difference between 34k and 38k just doesn't matter for nine out of 10 games here.

It's not about chairback seating numbers nowadays, it's the experiences and those who go want an experience.

If you go to the K today even for say a midweek game, the hangouts at Craft and Draft and Rivals bar are among the most popular spots. Like there isn't enough seating for general tickets to sit at either place. Buying a table seat or bench with loaded value are popular options. More bars and seating are a staple at big market parks. The K has the monopoly on bars in the area today, can certainly imagine these experiences will get much more attention.

The Diamond Club has good amount of indoor seating to get out of the sun if you wanted to table up with pals and watch the game before going back out behind home plate. Or the server takes your order seat side and brings it to you, I've always liked this experience the most.

Community America Club could certainly use an upgrade, plenty of round tables and the general buffet down there to mingle but you have to leave the area to really watch the game. I can totally imagine this being re-envisioned as the crown jewel of the new park.

The emphasis on premium experiences is the right way to go. College football has done the same things, get slightly smaller for more premium.

Advertising presented to you on this service can be based on limited data, such as the website or app you are using, your non-precise location, your device type or which content you are (or have been) interacting with (for example, to limit the number of times an ad is presented to you).

Use profiles to select personalised advertising 91 partners can use this purpose

Advertising presented to you on this service can be based on your advertising profiles, which can reflect your activity on this service or other websites or apps (like the forms you submit, content you look at), possible interests and personal aspects.

Create profiles for personalised advertising 95 partners can use this purpose

Information about your activity on this service (such as forms you submit, content you look at) can be stored and combined with other information about you (for example, information from your previous activity on this service and other websites or apps) or similar users. This is then used to build or improve a profile about you (that might include possible interests and personal aspects). Your profile can be used (also later) to present advertising that appears more relevant based on your possible interests by this and other entities.

Store and/or access information on a device 134 partners can use this purpose

Cookies, device or similar online identifiers (e.g. login-based identifiers, randomly assigned identifiers, network based identifiers) together with other information (e.g. browser type and information, language, screen size, supported technologies etc.) can be stored or read on your device to recognise it each time it connects to an app or to a website, for one or several of the purposes presented here.

Save and communicate privacy choices 106 partners can use this special purpose

Essential

The choices you make regarding the purposes and entities listed in this notice are saved and made available to those entities in the form of digital signals (such as a string of characters). This is necessary in order to enable both this service and those entities to respect such choices.
